# Dockerfile for lammps-reax on a CPU target
# Base Image: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS for a modern, stable environment
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set DEBIAN_FRONTEND to noninteractive to prevent prompts during package installation
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Configure OpenMPI for containerized environments.
# These settings are crucial for running MPI applications inside containers,
# especially in environments like Kubernetes.
# Allow running MPI processes as the root user.
ENV OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1
ENV OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1
# Disable searching for high-speed interconnects like InfiniBand which are not present.
ENV OMPI_MCA_btl="^openib"
# Use the OB1 PML (Point-to-Point Messaging Layer), a reliable default.
ENV OMPI_MCA_pml="ob1"
# This setting can prevent hangs related to shared memory transport (BTL vader) in some container runtimes.
ENV OMPI_MCA_btl_vader_single_copy_mechanism=none

# Install dependencies, clone, build LAMMPS, and clean up in a single RUN command
# This minimizes the number of layers in the final Docker image.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    gfortran \
    git \
    ca-certificates \
    libopenmpi-dev \
    openmpi-bin \
    libfftw3-dev \
    libgomp1 \
    # FIX: Add python3 to satisfy the LAMMPS cmake build dependency.
    python3 \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    # FIX: Clone the 'develop' branch to get the latest version as requested.
    && git clone --depth 1 -b develop https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git /opt/lammps-src \
    && cd /opt/lammps-src \
    && mkdir build && cd build \
    # Configure the LAMMPS build with CMake
    # Enable MPI, REAXFF, and other common packages for general-purpose simulations
    && cmake ../cmake \
      -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -D BUILD_MPI=yes \
      -D PKG_REAXFF=yes \
      -D PKG_MOLECULE=yes \
      -D PKG_KSPACE=yes \
    # Compile LAMMPS using all available processor cores
    && make -j$(nproc) \
    # Copy the compiled LAMMPS executable to a standard location in the system PATH
    && cp ./lmp /usr/local/bin/lmp \
    # Create the final working directory
    && mkdir -p /data \
    # Copy the HNS reaxff example files into the working directory
    && cp /opt/lammps-src/examples/reaxff/HNS/* /data/ \
    # Clean up the source code to reduce the final image size
    && rm -rf /opt/lammps-src

# Set the final working directory for the container
WORKDIR /data

# This MiniCluster manifest is designed for a single-node, multi-task HPC experiment
# running a LAMMPS simulation on an AWS CPU instance within Kubernetes.
# It is configured to be deployed by the Flux Operator.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name of the MiniCluster deployment.
  name: lammps-reaxff-hns-experiment
  # Deploys to the 'default' namespace as none is specified.
spec:
  # Specify the number of pods to create for the MiniCluster.
  # For this single AWS instance experiment, we request 1 pod.
  size: 1

  # The total number of tasks (e.g., MPI ranks) for the job.
  # Flux will run this many copies of the command across the allocated pods.
  tasks: 4

  # Defines the container that will run the HPC application.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      # The command to be executed by Flux. The operator wraps this in `flux run -n <tasks> ...`
      command: lmp -v x 2 -v y 2 -v z 2 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite
      # Per instructions, this container is a participant in the Flux instance
      # but does not drive the job submission itself.
      launcher: false

  # Logging settings for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Enforces strict schema validation for the logs.
    strict: true

  # Job completion policy.
  # When set to false, the MiniCluster pods and resources are not deleted
  # after the job completes, allowing for post-run inspection.
  cleanup: false

# This MiniCluster manifest is corrected to prevent Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors
# by selecting an AWS instance type with more memory.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  name: lammps-reaxff-hns-experiment
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The job will run within a single pod.
  size: 1

  # The number of tasks (e.g., MPI ranks) is set to 64 for a large-scale run.
  tasks: 64

  # Defines the application container.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      # The command is configured for the 64-task simulation (8x8 grid).
      command: lmp -v x 8 -v y 8 -v z 8 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite
      # This container is a worker, not the launcher.
      launcher: false

  # Custom flux container configuration.
  flux:
    container:
      # Use a flux-view image compatible with the ARM architecture of the Graviton instance.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-rocky:arm-9

  # Pod-level specifications.
  pod:
    # A nodeSelector is used to schedule the pod onto a memory-optimized instance.
    # The m7g.16xlarge instance provides 256 GiB of memory for the 64 CPUs,
    # addressing the OOM issues seen on instances with less RAM.
    nodeSelector:
      node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: m7g.16xlarge

  # Logging settings for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    strict: true

  # When set to false, the MiniCluster resources are not deleted after job completion,
  # allowing for post-mortem analysis.
  cleanup: false

updates.reason: The previous time of 10s was for a much smaller 2x2x2 problem. This is the first attempt on the target 8x8x8 problem size. I am selecting the top-tier HPC Graviton instance (hpc7g.16xlarge) and maximizing core utilization with 64 tasks to establish a strong performance baseline.

The previous run on a 64-core ARM instance (m7g.16xlarge) resulted in a 28-second wall time. This attempt will test the performance on a comparable high-end, 48-core AMD (x86) instance (c7a.12xlarge) to see if a different CPU architecture provides better results for this specific LAMMPS workload.

The best time so far is 28s on the 64-core hpc7g.16xlarge (ARM) instance. The 48-core c7a.12xlarge (AMD) was slower at 33s, indicating that either the ARM architecture or the higher core count is beneficial. To test for negative scaling effects (e.g., communication overhead or memory bandwidth contention), this attempt will run on the best-performing hpc7g.16xlarge instance but with a reduced task count of 48 to see if oversaturation was a limiting factor.

The best time of 28s was achieved on a 64-core Graviton3 instance (m7g.16xlarge) fully saturated with 64 tasks. Subsequent attempts on a comparable AMD instance (c7a.12xlarge, 33s) and on a similar ARM instance with fewer tasks (hpc7g.16xlarge, 33s) both resulted in worse performance. This indicates that for this workload, the ARM architecture combined with a high degree of parallelism provides the optimal configuration. Further iterations are unlikely to yield significant improvements. The optimal configuration found is 64 tasks on a 64-core Graviton3 instance.
